rel: Outcome means result. Reviewing past results to improve is like analysing errors in learning.

question: Choose the antonym of IMAGINARY.
facts: Imaginary means existing only in the mind; its opposite is Real. B) Fanciful, C) Fictional and D) Unreal are wrong: they all mean not real, the same as imaginary.
rel: Other antonyms: actual, factual, existing. Do not confuse imaginary (not real) with imaginative (creative).

question: Synonym of "rapid" is:
facts: 'Rapid' means very fast, so 'swift' is the synonym. A) 'slow' is the opposite. C) 'late' means after the right time, not speed. D) 'weak' means lacking strength.
rel: Other synonyms: quick, speedy, fast, hasty. Antonyms: slow, sluggish.

question: "He waited for ___ hour."
facts: The h in 'hour' is silent, so it begins with a vowel sound and takes 'an'. A) 'a' is wrong: 'a' is for consonant sounds. C) 'the' is wrong: no specific hour is meant. D) is wrong: 'hour' is a singular countable noun and needs an article.
rel: Silent h: an hour, an honest man, an heir, an honour. Pronounced h: a hospital, a hero, a historic day.

question: Choose the synonym of WICKED.
facts: Wicked means very bad; its synonym is Evil. A) Virtuous, C) Kind and D) Noble are wrong: they mean good, the opposite.
rel: Other synonyms: sinful, vicious, cruel. Antonym: virtuous (see sa-24).

question: "I ___ this book since Monday."
facts: 'Since Monday' shows an action that started in the past and is still going on, so present perfect continuous 'have been reading' is correct. A) 'read' is wrong: simple tense does not show continuation till now. B) 'am reading' is wrong: present continuous cannot be used with 'since'. D) 'had read' is wrong: past perfect needs another past event.
rel: Present perfect continuous: have/has been + verb-ing, with since (point of time) or for (period). Example: She has been waiting for two hours.

question: "___ Quran is the holy book of Islam."
facts: Names of well-known holy books take 'the', so 'The Quran'. A) 'A' and B) 'An' are wrong: there is only one Quran, not any one of many. D) is wrong: the name is used with 'the' by convention.
rel: Similarly: the Bible, the Torah, the Gita. Some famous newspapers too: the Times, the Guardian.

question: Complete: "He left early ___ avoid the traffic."
facts: A is right: 'in order to' + base verb shows purpose: he left early to avoid traffic. B) 'because' needs a full clause (because he wanted to avoid). C) 'although' shows contrast and needs a clause. D) 'despite' shows contrast and needs a noun or -ing, not 'avoid'.
rel: Other purpose forms: to, so as to, so that (He left early so that he could avoid the traffic). Negative: so as not to, in order not to.

question: Choose the antonym of EQUAL.
facts: Equal means the same in size, amount or level; its opposite is Uneven (not the same). A) Same, B) Uniform and D) Identical are wrong: they all mean alike, like equal.
rel: Other antonyms: unequal, different, unlike. In sa-76, Uniform is a synonym of equal.

question: He said, "May you succeed!"
options: He prayed that I might succeed.
He said that I may succeeded.
facts: A wish or prayer (May you...) is reported with 'prayed/wished that' + 'might': He prayed that I might succeed. B) keeps 'may' and uses 'succeeded'; after a modal use the base form. C) 'asked me to succeeding' is wrong form and wrong verb. D) 'ordered success' changes the meaning; a prayer is not an order.
rel: Same rule: She said, 'May God bless you' becomes She prayed that God might bless me. 'May' becomes 'might'.

question: Antonym of "frequent" is:
facts: "Frequent" means happening often, so its antonym is "rare" (happening seldom). A) "common", B) "regular" and D) "repeated" all have meanings close to frequent, so they are synonyms, not opposites.
rel: Other antonyms of frequent: infrequent, occasional, uncommon. Adverb pair: frequently versus rarely or seldom.

question: "Listen! Someone ___ at the door."
facts: 'Listen!' shows the knocking is happening right now, so present continuous 'is knocking' is correct. A) 'knocks' is wrong: simple present is for habits. B) 'knocked' is wrong: it is past. D) 'has knocked' is wrong: it shows a completed action, not one in progress.
rel: Clue words for present continuous: Look!, Listen!, now, at the moment. Example: Look! The children are playing.

question: "She is ___ best candidate in the group."
facts: Superlative adjectives (best, tallest, most famous) take 'the', so 'the best candidate'. A) 'a' and B) 'an' are wrong: a superlative points to one specific person, not any one. D) is wrong: a superlative normally needs 'the'.
rel: Examples: the tallest boy, the most intelligent student, the highest peak. Also 'the' with ordinal numbers: the first, the second.

question: "Sustain" most nearly means:
facts: A is right: 'sustain' means to keep something going or to maintain it. B) 'destroy' is the opposite. C) 'forget' is unrelated. D) 'interrupt' means to stop for a while, which is nearly the opposite.
rel: Synonyms: maintain, uphold, support, continue. Related: 'sustainable development' means growth that can be kept going; 'sustain an injury' means to suffer an injury.

question: "He arrived ___ the airport on time."
facts: We use 'arrive at' for a specific place or building like an airport, station or school. A) 'arrive in' is used for a city or country (arrive in Lahore). C) 'arrive on' is not used for places; 'on' is for days (arrive on Monday). D) 'arrive by' shows the means or a deadline (arrive by train, by 5 pm), not the place.
rel: Remember: arrive at the station/office, arrive in Karachi/Pakistan. 'Reach' takes no preposition: He reached the airport.

question: "Adaptable" means:
facts: A is right: 'adaptable' means able to adjust or change to fit new conditions. B) 'unable to change' is the opposite meaning. C) 'careless' means not paying attention, a different idea. D) 'slow only' has no link to the word.
rel: Synonyms: flexible, versatile, adjustable. Antonyms: rigid, inflexible. Do not confuse adapt (adjust) with adopt (take as your own).

question: Choose the synonym of REASON.
facts: As a verb, reason means to think and discuss logically, to argue a point; so Argue is the synonym. B) Ignore is wrong: it means to pay no attention. C) Accede is wrong: it means to agree to a demand. D) Obey is wrong: it means to follow orders.
rel: Phrase: to reason with someone means to try to persuade them by argument. Other synonyms: deduce, infer, think.

question: Choose the antonym of MAJORITY.
facts: Majority means the larger part or number; its opposite is Minority (the smaller part). A) Plurality, C) Bulk and D) Mass are wrong: they all refer to the larger part or a big amount.
rel: Same pattern: major - minor, majority - minority. Majority means more than half.

question: Choose the antonym of ABILITY.
facts: Ability means power or skill to do something; its opposite is Incapability (not being able). A) Capability, B) Skill and C) Talent are wrong: they all mean ability.
rel: Other antonyms: inability, incapacity, incompetence. In sa-43, Capability is a synonym of ability.

question: In the same sentence, "omission" most nearly means:
facts: A is right: an omission is something left out or forgotten. B) a reward is a prize, not related. C) an explanation is giving reasons. D) a prediction is a guess about the future.
rel: Verb: omit (to leave out). Similar words: exclusion, oversight, gap. Opposite: inclusion, addition.

question: Which of the following is a conjunction?
facts: 'Because' joins two clauses and gives a reason, so it is a (subordinating) conjunction. A) 'under' is wrong: it is a preposition of place. C) 'quickly' is wrong: it is an adverb of manner. D) 'brave' is wrong: it is an adjective.
rel: Other subordinating conjunctions: since, as, although, though, unless, if, when, while. Example: He stayed home because he was ill.

question: "We crossed ___ Indus River."
facts: Names of rivers take 'the', so it is 'the Indus River'. A) 'a' and B) 'an' are wrong: a particular named river is not 'any one'. D) is wrong: river names are not used without 'the'.
rel: Also with 'the': seas, oceans, canals and deserts - the Arabian Sea, the Pacific Ocean, the Suez Canal, the Thar Desert.

question: "He ___ for two hours before the rain stopped."
facts: 'For two hours before the rain stopped' stresses how long an action continued before another past event, so past perfect continuous 'had been running' is correct. A) 'ran' is wrong: it does not show duration before another past event. C) 'has been running' is wrong: it links to the present, not the past. D) 'is running' is wrong: it is present.
rel: Past perfect continuous: had been + verb-ing. Example: She had been waiting for an hour when the bus came.

question: Indirect: He said, "What a beautiful view!"
options: He exclaimed that it was a very beautiful view.
He asked whether the view was beautiful.
He said what was a view?
facts: An exclamation is reported with "exclaimed that" and changed into a statement: "He exclaimed that it was a very beautiful view." The word "What" becomes "very". B) "asked whether" turns it into a question, which is wrong. C) "ordered" is for commands. D) "said what was a view?" keeps a question form and makes no sense.
rel: Other exclamations: He said, "Hurrah! We won" becomes He exclaimed with joy that they had won. "Alas!" is reported with "exclaimed with sorrow".

question: "The train passed ___ the tunnel."
facts: 'Through' is used for moving inside something from one end to the other, like a tunnel, pipe or forest. The train went in one end and came out the other. B) 'across' is for moving from one side of a flat surface to the other, like a road or river. C) 'over' means above, but a train goes inside a tunnel, not above it. D) 'beside' means next to, which is not movement inside.
rel: Other examples: walk through the forest, look through the window, read through the book. Compare: walk across the road, fly over the city.

question: Passive of "They are building a bridge" is:
options: A bridge is being built by them.
A bridge was built by them.
A bridge has been built by them.
facts: Present continuous active (are building) becomes 'is/are being + past participle' in passive: A bridge is being built by them. B) 'was built' is simple past, wrong tense. C) 'has been built' is present perfect, wrong tense. D) 'is built them' misses 'being' and the word 'by', and is the wrong tense.
rel: Same rule: She is cooking food becomes Food is being cooked by her. Past continuous: was/were being + past participle.

question: "Concise" means:
facts: A is right: concise means brief but complete, saying a lot in few words. B) 'very confusing' is wrong: that is muddled or obscure. C) 'lengthy' is wrong: it is the opposite (verbose, wordy). D) 'careless' is wrong: that is negligent, not about length.
rel: Synonyms of concise: succinct, terse, brief, pithy, to the point. Antonyms: verbose, wordy, long-winded, prolix.

question: Passive of "You should follow the instructions" is:
facts: With a modal verb, the passive is modal + be + past participle: "The instructions should be followed." B) "should followed" is missing "be". C) "are should follow" puts two verbs wrongly together; a modal never follows "are". D) "The instructions followed you" changes the meaning and is not passive.
rel: Same rule with other modals: "You must finish the work" becomes "The work must be finished." "We can solve it" becomes "It can be solved."

question: Choose the synonym of RESCIND.
facts: Rescind means to cancel a law, order or agreement; its synonym is Cancel. B) Enact, C) Approve and D) Confirm are wrong: they mean make or keep valid, the opposite.
rel: Other synonyms: revoke, repeal, annul, withdraw. Antonyms: enact, validate.

question: Neither Ali ___ Hamza was late.
facts: C is right: 'neither' is always paired with 'nor': neither ... nor. A) 'and' is wrong: it pairs with 'both'. B) 'or' is wrong: it pairs with 'either'. D) 'but' is wrong: it is not a partner of 'neither'.
rel: With neither ... nor, the verb agrees with the nearer subject: 'Neither the teacher nor the students were late.' Same for either ... or.

question: A writer says, "The plan is costly; nevertheless, it may be necessary." "Nevertheless" signals:
facts: A is right: 'nevertheless' means 'in spite of that', so it shows contrast between 'costly' and 'necessary'. B) cause words are because or since. C) time words are then, later, after. D) addition words are also, moreover, furthermore.
rel: Similar contrast words: however, nonetheless, still, even so, yet. Example: He was ill; nonetheless, he came to work.

question: Choose the antonym of "scarce".
facts: 'Scarce' means not enough or hard to find, so the antonym is 'abundant' (more than enough). A) 'rare' is a synonym, not an antonym. B) 'limited' also means not much, a synonym. D) 'small' is about size and is close in meaning, not opposite.
rel: Other antonyms: plentiful, ample. Noun: scarcity (shortage), abundance (plenty).

question: He is responsible ___ the equipment.
facts: The fixed phrase is "responsible for" something or someone. A) "of" is wrong with responsible. B) "to" is used for the person you report to: "responsible to the manager", not for the equipment. D) "at" is not used with responsible.
rel: Other adjectives with "for": famous for, ready for, eligible for, grateful for (something). Example: "Lahore is famous for its food."

question: "At 8 p.m. yesterday, we ___ for the test."
facts: An action that was going on at a fixed past time (8 p.m. yesterday) uses past continuous 'were studying'. A) 'studied' is wrong: it shows a completed action, not one in progress at that moment. C) 'have studied' is wrong: present perfect cannot be used with 'yesterday'. D) 'study' is wrong: it is present tense.
rel: Past continuous: was/were + verb-ing. Example: At 10 a.m. she was writing a letter. Also used for an interrupted action: I was reading when he came.

question: Synonym of "brave" is:
facts: 'Brave' means not afraid of danger, so 'courageous' is the synonym. A) 'cowardly' is the opposite (antonym). C) 'weak' means lacking strength, not the same. D) 'silent' means quiet and has no link to bravery.
rel: Other synonyms: bold, fearless, daring, valiant, gallant. Antonyms: cowardly, timid, fearful.

question: "Pakistan became independent ___ 1947."
facts: Use 'in' for years: in 1947. B) 'on' is wrong: 'on' is for days and dates. C) 'at' is wrong: 'at' is for clock time. D) 'since' is wrong: it goes with perfect tenses (has been independent since 1947).
rel: 'In' is used with months, years, seasons, centuries: in August, in 1947, in summer, in the 20th century. But 'on 14 August 1947' with a full date.

question: In reported questions, the word order is generally:
facts: In reported questions we use statement order (subject + verb), not question order: He asked where she lived, not where did she live. A) question order is used only in direct speech. C) 'inverted twice' is not a grammar rule. D) 'verb only' is wrong; the clause needs a subject too.
rel: Example: 'Is he coming?' becomes She asked if he was coming. 'Why are you sad?' becomes He asked why I was sad.

question: "The plane flew ___ the clouds."
facts: 'Above' means at a higher level, so the plane flew above the clouds. B) 'between only' is wrong: 'between' needs two things and 'only' makes it ungrammatical. C) 'beside' is wrong: it means next to, at the side. D) 'since' is wrong: it is for time, not place.
rel: Above vs over: above = higher than (the plane is above the clouds); over = covering or crossing (a bridge over the river). Opposite: below/under.

question: The team consists ___ ten members.
facts: The fixed phrase is "consist of", meaning to be made up of. A) "consist in" is a different, formal phrase meaning "to have as the main part" and does not fit here. C) "on" and D) "at" are not used with consist.
rel: Similar phrases: "be composed of" and "be made up of" mean the same: "Water is composed of hydrogen and oxygen." Note: we never say "is consisted of".

question: Read the passage: Efficient reading is not the same as reading every line at maximum speed. Skilled readers vary their pace according to purpose. They may scan a page to locate a date, skim an article to grasp its main argument, or read slowly when a paragraph contains dense reasoning. They also monitor comprehension. If a key sentence is unclear, they pause, reread, and connect it with surrounding ideas. This flexible approach is especially useful in timed tests, where spending too long on one difficult sentence can reduce the time available for easier questions.  QUESTION: Efficient readers vary their pace according to:
facts: B is right: the passage says 'Skilled readers vary their pace according to purpose.' A) 'page color' is wrong: not mentioned. C) 'handwriting' is wrong: not mentioned. D) 'mood only' is wrong: not mentioned.
rel: Pace means speed. Purpose decides the method: scan for facts, skim for the main idea, read slowly for dense reasoning.

question: Synonym of "robust" is:
facts: "Robust" means strong and healthy, so its synonym is "strong". B) "fragile" means easily broken, which is the opposite. C) "silent" means quiet, not related. D) "rare" means not common, not related.
rel: Other synonyms of robust: sturdy, tough, vigorous, hardy. Antonyms: weak, frail, delicate.

question: Choose the synonym of DETERMINATION.
facts: Determination means firm decision to do something; its synonym is Resolution. A) Weakness, B) Hesitation and C) Doubt are wrong: they show lack of firmness, the opposite.
rel: Other synonyms: resolve, firmness, willpower. A New Year resolution is a firm decision to do something.

question: Choose the antonym of ATTRACT.
facts: Attract means to pull towards; its opposite is Repel (push away). A) Charm, C) Allure and D) Draw are wrong: they all mean to attract or pull in.
rel: In magnets, like poles repel and unlike poles attract. Noun pair: attraction - repulsion (see sa-25).

question: Choose the antonym of WICKED.
facts: Wicked means evil or very bad; its opposite is Virtuous (good, moral). A) Cruel, B) Evil and D) Sinful are wrong: they all mean bad, like wicked.
rel: Other antonyms: righteous, noble, good. In sa-57, Evil is a synonym of wicked.

question: Read the passage: Errors are unavoidable in serious learning. Their value, however, depends on what happens after they are noticed. Repeating an error without analysis produces little improvement. Effective learners identify the cause, correct the method, and test the correction under similar conditions. They also distinguish between a careless mistake and a conceptual misunderstanding. The first may require better attention; the second may require rebuilding knowledge from the foundation. This process can feel slower than simply doing more questions, but it usually produces more durable progress because it changes the mechanism that caused the failure.  QUESTION: A conceptual misunderstanding may require:
facts: B is right: the passage says a conceptual misunderstanding 'may require rebuilding knowledge from the foundation'. A) 'more speed only' is wrong: speed is not mentioned as a fix. C) 'less attention' is wrong: careless mistakes need better (more) attention. D) 'memorizing the same answer' is wrong: it does not fix the concept.
rel: Careless mistake = slip in attention; conceptual misunderstanding = wrong idea of the topic. Foundation means the basic level.

question: Passive of "They were watching the match" is:
options: The match was being watched by them.
facts: Past continuous active (were watching) becomes 'was/were being + past participle': The match was being watched by them. A) 'was watched' is simple past, it loses 'being'. C) 'is being watched' is present continuous, wrong tense. D) 'has been watched' is present perfect, wrong tense.
rel: Same rule: She was cooking food becomes Food was being cooked by her. Present continuous version: is/are being + past participle.

question: "Adverse" means:
facts: B is right: adverse means harmful or unfavourable, e.g. adverse weather or adverse effects. A) 'favorable' is wrong: it is the opposite. C) 'equal' is wrong: that means the same. D) 'pleasant' is wrong: that is nice or agreeable.
rel: Synonyms of adverse: unfavourable, harmful, hostile, detrimental. Do not confuse with 'averse' (unwilling): 'He is averse to risk.' Noun: adversity (hard times).

question: Read the passage: Errors are unavoidable in serious learning. Their value, however, depends on what happens after they are noticed. Repeating an error without analysis produces little improvement. Effective learners identify the cause, correct the method, and test the correction under similar conditions. They also distinguish between a careless mistake and a conceptual misunderstanding. The first may require better attention; the second may require rebuilding knowledge from the foundation. This process can feel slower than simply doing more questions, but it usually produces more durable progress because it changes the mechanism that caused the failure.  QUESTION: The phrase "durable progress" most nearly means progress that is:
facts: B is right: durable means long-lasting, so durable progress is progress that lasts. A) 'temporary' is wrong: it is the opposite. C) 'accidental' is wrong: the progress comes from a careful method. D) 'rapid only' is wrong: the passage says the method 'can feel slower'.
rel: Synonyms of durable: lasting, enduring, permanent, long-lasting. Antonyms: temporary, fleeting, short-lived.

question: Antonym of "superior" is:
facts: 'Superior' means higher in rank or better in quality, so the antonym is 'inferior' (lower or worse). A) 'higher' is a synonym. B) 'better' is a synonym. D) 'excellent' is close in meaning.
rel: Both take 'to', not 'than': superior to, inferior to. Similar pair: senior to vs. junior to.

question: "This book belongs ___ me."
facts: The verb 'belong' takes 'to': belongs to me. A) 'with', B) 'for' and D) 'at' are wrong: they do not go with 'belong' in this meaning of ownership.
rel: Other verb + to: listen to, reply to, object to, refer to. 'Belong' is a stative verb, so not 'is belonging'.

question: Passive of "The committee may approve the plan" is:
options: The plan may be approved by the committee.
facts: Modal passive is 'may + be + past participle': The plan may be approved by the committee. B) misses 'be'. C) 'is may approve' puts two helping verbs wrongly and is not passive. D) 'may been' is wrong; after a modal we use 'be', and 'been' needs 'have' (may have been).
rel: Same rule: They can solve the problem becomes The problem can be solved. Past modal passive: may have been approved.

question: Passive of "The mechanic repaired the vehicle" is:
options: The vehicle was repaired by the mechanic.
facts: The active is simple past, so the passive uses was/were + past participle: "The vehicle was repaired by the mechanic." A) "The vehicle repaired" has no "was", so it wrongly says the vehicle did the repairing. C) "is repair" uses the wrong tense and the base form instead of the past participle. D) "The mechanic was repaired" reverses the meaning.
rel: Same rule: "She wrote a letter" becomes "A letter was written by her." Plural object uses were: "They built houses" becomes "Houses were built by them."

question: Choose the synonym of ABILITY.
facts: Ability means power or skill to do something; its synonym is Capability. B) Weakness, C) Inability and D) Failure are wrong: they are opposite in meaning to ability.
rel: Other synonyms: skill, talent, competence, capacity. Antonym: inability (see sa-29).

question: Choose the antonym of COMFORT.
facts: Comfort means ease and relief from pain or worry; its opposite is Oppression (hard and cruel treatment, burden). A) Relief, B) Ease and C) Solace are wrong: they all mean comfort.
rel: Other antonyms of comfort: distress, discomfort, misery. Solace means comfort in sadness.

question: Which is correct?
facts: "Useful" starts with a "yu" sound, which is a consonant sound, so "a useful tool" is correct. A) "an useful" is wrong because "an" is only for vowel sounds. C) "the useful tool always" is not a correct phrase; "always" makes no sense here. D) "useful an tool" has the wrong word order: the article must come before the adjective.
rel: Same rule: a university, a unit, a union. But "an umbrella" and "an uncle" take "an" because they start with an "uh" vowel sound.

question: Choose the synonym of DANGER.
facts: Danger means the chance of harm; its synonym is Risk. A) Shelter, B) Safety and D) Security are wrong: they mean being protected, the opposite.
rel: Other synonyms: hazard, peril, threat. Antonym: safety (see sa-26).

question: A paragraph whose examples all support one claim has strong:
facts: A is right: unity means every part of a paragraph supports one main idea or claim. B) ambiguity means unclear, with two possible meanings. C) contradiction means parts that go against each other. D) inversion means changing the normal word order.
rel: Related writing ideas: coherence (ideas flow logically with good links) and topic sentence (the sentence that gives the main claim).

question: "She is interested ___ military history."
facts: The fixed phrase is 'interested in' something. A) 'on', B) 'at' and D) 'for' are wrong: they do not go with 'interested'.
rel: Similar collocations: keen on, fond of, good at, aware of, proud of. Example: He is fond of reading.

question: He apologized ___ being late.
facts: The fixed phrase is "apologize for" something (the reason). B) "of" does not go with apologize. C) "with" does not go with apologize. D) "to" is used for the person: "apologize to someone", not for the reason.
rel: Full pattern: "He apologized to the teacher for being late." Similar: thank someone for, blame someone for, forgive someone for.

question: If a passage states evidence first and a conclusion later, the reader should:
options: distinguish the supporting evidence from the conclusion
treat every sentence as identical in function
assume the first sentence is always the conclusion
facts: A is right: a good reader separates the evidence (support) from the conclusion it leads to. B) wrong: sentences have different jobs, so they are not identical. C) wrong: connectors like 'therefore' and 'so' show where the conclusion starts. D) wrong: here the conclusion comes later, so the first sentence is not always the conclusion.
rel: Conclusion signal words: therefore, thus, hence, so, consequently. Evidence signal words: because, since, for example, studies show.

question: Change to passive: "The officer signed the document."
options: The document was signed by the officer.
The document is signed by the officer yesterday.
The officer was signed by the document.
facts: The active sentence is simple past, so the passive uses 'was/were + past participle': The document was signed by the officer. A) is wrong: without 'was' it means the document did the signing. C) is wrong: 'is signed' is present tense and does not match 'yesterday' or the past tense. D) is wrong: it swaps the doer and the object, so the meaning becomes nonsense.
rel: Same rule: She wrote a poem becomes A poem was written by her. Plural object: He bought two books becomes Two books were bought by him.

question: Choose the synonym of LAUD.
facts: Laud means to praise highly; its synonym is Praise. B) Blame, C) Condemn and D) Criticize are wrong: they are opposite in meaning.
rel: Other synonyms: extol, acclaim, applaud. Laudable means worthy of praise.

question: Choose the antonym of WANT.
facts: Here want means poverty or lack of things; its opposite is Prosperity (wealth, having plenty). A) Need, B) Shortage and D) Poverty are wrong: they all mean the same as want.
rel: Other antonyms: plenty, wealth, abundance. Phrase: to live in want means to live in poverty.

question: The word "but" in "He was tired but continued" is a:
facts: 'But' joins two parts of equal rank and shows contrast, so it is a coordinating conjunction. A) subordinating conjunction is wrong: those (although, because) start a dependent clause. C) preposition is wrong: here no noun object follows it. D) interjection is wrong: it shows no emotion.
rel: Contrast words: but, yet (coordinating); although, though, whereas (subordinating); however (linking adverb). Example: He was tired, yet he continued.

question: "Deterrent" means something that:
facts: A is right: a deterrent is something that discourages people or stops them from doing something, e.g. heavy fines are a deterrent to crime. B) a deterrent does not promise a reward; that is an incentive. C) it does not increase confusion. D) recording history is a record or archive, not a deterrent.
rel: Verb: deter (to discourage). Opposite idea: incentive or motivation, which encourages an action. Example: Nuclear weapons are called a deterrent.

question: He is proud ___ his achievement.
facts: A is right: the adjective 'proud' is followed by 'of'. B) 'from', C) 'with' and D) 'at' are wrong prepositions with 'proud'.
rel: Other adjectives with 'of': afraid of, fond of, aware of, jealous of, capable of. Example: She is fond of reading.

question: Indirect questions use:
facts: Indirect questions are not real questions, so they use statement word order: subject before verb, e.g. "He asked where I lived" (not "where did I live"). B) "question inversion" is used in direct questions only. C) An indirect question still has a verb. D) The tense depends on the reporting verb, not "only past perfect".
rel: Same rule: Direct "Where is the bank?" becomes "Can you tell me where the bank is?" Yes/no questions use if or whether: "She asked if I was ready."

question: Choose the synonym of FERVOUR.
facts: Fervour means strong, warm feeling or enthusiasm; its synonym is Zeal. A) Indifference, B) Coldness and D) Apathy are wrong: they mean lack of interest, the opposite.
rel: Other synonyms: passion, ardour, enthusiasm. Adjectives: fervent, zealous.

question: Antonym of "conceal" is:
facts: 'Conceal' means to hide, so the antonym is 'reveal' (to show or make known). A) 'hide' is a synonym. B) 'cover' is close to hide. D) 'protect' means to keep safe, not the opposite.
rel: Other antonyms: disclose, expose, show. Synonyms: hide, mask, cover up.

question: In "This is the man who helped us," "who" is a:
facts: 'Who' refers back to 'the man' and starts the clause 'who helped us', so it is a relative pronoun. B) article is wrong: articles are only a, an, the. C) preposition is wrong: it shows no relation of place or time. D) interjection is wrong: it shows no feeling.
rel: Relative pronouns: who (people), which (things), that (people or things), whom, whose. Example: The book which I bought is new.

question: Choose the antonym of SUPPORT.
facts: Support means to help or hold up; its opposite is Abandon (leave and stop helping). A) Help, C) Assist and D) Uphold are wrong: they all mean the same as support.
rel: Other antonyms of support: oppose, desert, undermine. Synonyms: back, aid, sustain.

question: Passive of "Who wrote this letter?" is:
options: By whom was this letter written?
This letter was wrote by whom?
facts: A 'who' question in passive starts with 'By whom' + was + subject + past participle: By whom was this letter written? B) uses 'who' instead of 'whom' after 'by' and has no 'was'. C) 'Whom wrote' is wrong; 'whom' cannot be the subject. D) uses 'wrote' instead of the past participle 'written'.
rel: Same rule: Who broke the glass? becomes By whom was the glass broken? Also: Who is calling you? becomes By whom are you being called?

question: Read the passage: A team is not effective merely because its members are individually talented. Performance depends on coordination: members must understand the objective, know their responsibilities, share relevant information, and adjust when another member encounters difficulty. Trust reduces the time spent checking whether others will perform basic duties, but trust does not mean the absence of accountability. Strong teams make standards clear and address problems early. They also avoid confusing agreement with unity. Members may disagree about methods while still remaining committed to the same mission.  QUESTION: The best title would be:
facts: B is right: the whole passage explains what makes a team effective: coordination, trust, accountability and shared mission. A) is wrong: the passage says talent is not enough, not useless. C) is wrong: the passage supports accountability. D) is wrong: the passage is about cooperation, not individual competition.
rel: A good title covers the main idea of the whole passage, not one detail, and avoids extreme words like 'useless' or 'only'.

question: "They ___ the task before the instructor arrived."
facts: Two past actions: finishing the task came first, so it takes past perfect 'had completed'; the later one is simple past 'arrived'. A) 'complete' is wrong: it is present tense. C) 'have completed' is wrong: present perfect does not fit with a past time clause. D) 'were completing' is wrong: it shows the work was still going on, not finished before.
rel: Past perfect pattern: had + past participle. Example: The train had left before we reached the station. 'Before' and 'after' are common clues.

question: "He went to ___ school to attend his class."
facts: He went to school for its main purpose (to study), so no article is used: 'went to school'. A) 'a' and B) 'an' are wrong: they would mean any one school building. C) 'the' is wrong: 'the' is used when we mean the building for another purpose.
rel: Same rule: go to bed, go to hospital (as a patient), go to church, go to prison (as a prisoner), go to college.

question: Choose the antonym of OWN.
facts: Here own means to admit or accept something; its opposite is Disclaim (refuse to accept or deny). A) Admit, B) Accept and D) Acknowledge are wrong: they all mean the same as own.
rel: Other antonyms: deny, disown, reject. In sa-77, Acknowledge is a synonym of own.

question: Read the passage: Errors are unavoidable in serious learning. Their value, however, depends on what happens after they are noticed. Repeating an error without analysis produces little improvement. Effective learners identify the cause, correct the method, and test the correction under similar conditions. They also distinguish between a careless mistake and a conceptual misunderstanding. The first may require better attention; the second may require rebuilding knowledge from the foundation. This process can feel slower than simply doing more questions, but it usually produces more durable progress because it changes the mechanism that caused the failure.  QUESTION: Which distinction does the passage recommend?
facts: B is right: the passage says learners 'distinguish between a careless mistake and a conceptual misunderstanding'. A) 'Easy and hard exams' is wrong: not mentioned. C) 'Teachers and students' is wrong: not mentioned. D) 'Written and oral work' is wrong: not mentioned.
rel: Distinguish means tell the difference between two things. Distinguish between A and B; distinguish A from B.

question: In "The very experienced instructor spoke calmly," "very" is a:
facts: "Very" tells us how experienced the instructor is. It modifies the adjective "experienced", and a word that modifies an adjective is an adverb. A) It is not a noun: it does not name a person, place or thing. C) It is not an adjective: it does not describe the noun "instructor" directly. D) It is not a preposition: it does not join a noun to other words.
rel: Other adverbs of degree: too, quite, extremely, so, rather. Example: "She is extremely clever" - "extremely" is an adverb modifying the adjective "clever".

question: Choose the antonym of MISLEAD.
facts: Mislead means to lead someone the wrong way or give a wrong idea; its opposite is Guide (show the right way). A) Confuse, B) Deceive and D) Misdirect are wrong: they all have the same meaning as mislead.
rel: The prefix mis- means wrongly: misguide, misinform, misunderstand. Antonyms of mislead also include direct and inform correctly.

question: If you heat ice, it ___.
facts: This is a general scientific fact, so we use the zero conditional: if + simple present, simple present. So "it melts". A) "melted" is past tense and does not fit a general truth. C) "will melted" is wrong: after "will" we use the base form (melt). D) "would melt always" is the second conditional form used for unreal situations, not facts.
rel: More zero conditional examples: "If you heat water to 100 degrees, it boils." "If it rains, the ground gets wet."

question: Choose the antonym of COMPLEX.
facts: Complex means having many parts and hard to understand, so its opposite is Uncomplicated (simple, easy). A) Intricate, B) Complicated and D) Puzzling are wrong: they all mean the same as complex, so they are synonyms, not antonyms.
rel: Other antonyms of complex: simple, easy, plain, straightforward. Synonyms: complicated, intricate, involved.

question: "Mitigate" means:
facts: A is right: mitigate means to make something less severe or less harmful. B) 'make worse' is wrong: it is the opposite (aggravate, exacerbate). C) 'ignore entirely' is wrong: mitigate means acting to reduce harm. D) 'measure exactly' is wrong: that is to quantify.
rel: Synonyms of mitigate: alleviate, lessen, ease, reduce, assuage. Antonyms: aggravate, worsen, intensify. Noun: mitigation.

question: Synonym of "diligent" is:
facts: 'Diligent' means careful and hardworking, so 'hardworking' is the synonym. A) 'lazy' is the opposite. C) 'careless' is also opposite in meaning. D) 'reckless' means not caring about danger.
rel: Other synonyms: industrious, sincere, painstaking. Antonyms: lazy, idle, negligent. Noun: diligence.

question: "The cat jumped ___ the wall."
facts: 'Over' shows movement above something and to the other side, which is what a jump across a wall does. B) 'jump at' means to attack or grab something quickly, not to cross it. C) 'since' is about time (since Monday), not place. D) 'between' needs two things (between two walls), so it does not fit 'the wall'.
rel: Similar: the horse jumped over the fence; the plane flew over the mountains. 'Above' shows position only, while 'over' can also show movement across.

question: Indirect: He said, "I must leave now." In ordinary backshift, "must" may become:
facts: A is right: in reported speech 'must' (meaning need or duty) usually changes to 'had to': He said that he had to leave then. B) 'has to yesterday' is wrong tense and wrong time word. C) 'musted' does not exist; 'must' has no past form. D) 'would leaving' is wrong: 'would' needs a base verb.
rel: Other backshifts: can to could, will to would, may to might, is to was. Also 'now' becomes 'then' and 'today' becomes 'that day'.

question: In "Courage inspires others," "Courage" is a:
facts: "Courage" is a quality; we cannot see or touch it, so it is an abstract noun. A) It is not a proper noun: it is not the name of a particular person or place and is not written with a capital in normal use. C) It is not a verb: the verb in the sentence is "inspires". D) It is not an adverb: it is the subject of the sentence.
rel: Other abstract nouns: honesty, love, freedom, wisdom, childhood. Many are made with endings like -ness, -dom, -hood, -ity (kindness, freedom, childhood, ability).

question: "The teacher distributed books ___ the students."
facts: Use 'among' for more than two people: among the students. A) 'between' is wrong: it is mainly for two. C) 'through' is wrong: it means passing from one end to the other. D) 'onto' is wrong: it means movement to a surface.
rel: Among the crowd, among friends, among the trees. 'Amongst' has the same meaning but is more formal.

question: Synonym of "terminate" is:
facts: 'Terminate' means to bring to an end, so 'end' is the synonym. A) 'continue' is the opposite. C) 'begin' is the opposite. D) 'expand' means to grow bigger.
rel: Other synonyms: finish, stop, conclude, cease. Antonyms: begin, start, commence. Noun: termination.

question: "Explicit" means:
facts: A is right: 'explicit' means stated clearly and directly, with nothing left hidden. B) 'hidden' is the opposite. C) 'uncertain' means not sure, not clear. D) 'impossible' is unrelated.
rel: Antonym: implicit (suggested but not said directly). Synonyms of explicit: clear, plain, direct, unambiguous.

question: Which sentence cannot normally be changed into passive voice?
facts: Only verbs with an object (transitive verbs) can be made passive. 'Sleep' has no object, so 'The baby slept' cannot be changed. A) 'wrote a letter' has an object, so: A letter was written by him. B) 'repaired the road' has an object: The road was repaired. D) 'completed the form' has an object: The form was completed by her.
rel: Other intransitive verbs with no passive: go, come, die, arrive, sleep, laugh (without 'at'). Example: He died cannot be passive.

question: Read the passage: A team is not effective merely because its members are individually talented. Performance depends on coordination: members must understand the objective, know their responsibilities, share relevant information, and adjust when another member encounters difficulty. Trust reduces the time spent checking whether others will perform basic duties, but trust does not mean the absence of accountability. Strong teams make standards clear and address problems early. They also avoid confusing agreement with unity. Members may disagree about methods while still remaining committed to the same mission.  QUESTION: Members can disagree about methods while still:
options: sharing commitment to the same mission
facts: A is right: the last line says members may disagree about methods 'while still remaining committed to the same mission'. B) 'having no unity' is wrong: the passage says agreement and unity are different, and unity stays. C) 'rejecting all standards' is wrong: strong teams make standards clear. D) 'avoiding communication' is wrong: members must share information.
rel: Unity means being together for one purpose; agreement means having the same opinion. You can disagree yet stay united.

question: "By the time the test started, I ___ my notes."
facts: B is right: reviewing was finished before another past action (the test started), so we use the past perfect 'had reviewed'. A) 'reviewed already now' mixes past with 'now' and is wrong. C) 'have review' is wrong: present perfect needs 'reviewed', and the time is past. D) 'will reviewing' is wrong: future does not fit and 'will' needs a base verb.
rel: 'By the time' + past simple usually goes with past perfect in the other clause. Example: By the time we reached the station, the train had left.

question: Choose the synonym of MOAT.
facts: A moat is a deep ditch, usually filled with water, around a castle or fort; its synonym is Ditch. B) Hill and C) Mound are wrong: they are raised land, not dug land. D) Wall is wrong: a wall is built up, though a moat is often near one.
rel: Other synonyms: trench, channel. Do not confuse moat with mote (a tiny particle of dust).

question: Antonym of "permanent" is:
facts: 'Permanent' means lasting forever or for a long time, so the antonym is 'temporary' (for a short time only). A) 'lasting' is a synonym. B) 'fixed' is close to permanent. D) 'stable' is also close in meaning.
rel: Other antonyms: transient, short-lived, momentary. Synonyms: everlasting, enduring, eternal.

question: Choose the synonym of APPROVAL.
facts: Approval means agreeing or giving permission; its synonym is Consent. B) Rejection, C) Denial and D) Refusal are wrong: they mean saying no, the opposite.
rel: Other synonyms: assent, sanction, permission. Antonym: disapproval (see sa-19).

question: In "Honesty is essential for leadership," the word "Honesty" is a:
facts: 'Honesty' is the name of a quality we cannot touch or see, so it is an abstract noun. A) verb is wrong: it shows no action. C) adjective is wrong: the adjective form is 'honest'. D) conjunction is wrong: it does not join words or clauses.
rel: Other abstract nouns: bravery, loyalty, kindness, freedom, wisdom. Many are made with -ness, -ty, -dom, -ship (kind - kindness, friend - friendship).

question: Choose the synonym of WANT.
facts: Want means lack or need of something; its synonym is Need. A) Wealth, B) Comfort and C) Excess are wrong: they mean having plenty, the opposite.
rel: Other synonyms: lack, poverty, shortage. Antonym: prosperity (see sa-32).

question: Which sentence contains an adverb of frequency?
facts: 'Often' tells how many times the action happens, so it is an adverb of frequency. A) 'yesterday' is wrong: it is an adverb of time. C) 'here' is wrong: it is an adverb of place. D) 'softly' is wrong: it is an adverb of manner.
rel: Adverbs of frequency: always, usually, often, sometimes, seldom, rarely, never. They usually come before the main verb: He often exercises.

question: Choose the antonym of FREEDOM.
facts: Freedom means being free; its opposite is Slavery (being owned or controlled). A) Liberty, C) Release and D) Independence are wrong: they all mean freedom.
rel: Other antonyms of freedom: bondage, captivity, servitude. Synonyms: liberty, independence, autonomy.

question: In "The book is on the desk," "on" is a:
facts: 'On' shows the position of the book in relation to the desk, so it is a preposition (it is followed by the noun 'the desk'). B) adverb is wrong: an adverb would have no noun object after it. C) interjection is wrong: it shows no feeling. D) pronoun is wrong: it does not replace a noun.
rel: Prepositions of place: on, in, at, under, above, beside, between. A preposition is always followed by a noun or pronoun (its object).

question: "Divide the sweets ___ the two boys."
facts: Use 'between' for two people or things: between the two boys. A) 'among' is wrong: it is for more than two. C) 'into' is wrong: it means movement inside or dividing into parts (divide into pieces). D) 'beside' is wrong: it means next to.
rel: Between for two (between you and me); among for more than two (among the students). 'Divide into' is for parts: divide the cake into four pieces.

question: Read the passage: Errors are unavoidable in serious learning. Their value, however, depends on what happens after they are noticed. Repeating an error without analysis produces little improvement. Effective learners identify the cause, correct the method, and test the correction under similar conditions. They also distinguish between a careless mistake and a conceptual misunderstanding. The first may require better attention; the second may require rebuilding knowledge from the foundation. This process can feel slower than simply doing more questions, but it usually produces more durable progress because it changes the mechanism that caused the failure.  QUESTION: The passage suggests that simply doing more questions can be inferior because it may:
options: fail to change the cause of error
facts: B is right: the careful method is better 'because it changes the mechanism that caused the failure', so doing more questions may leave the cause unchanged. A) 'be illegal' is wrong: nothing in the passage. C) 'always lower confidence' is wrong: confidence is not mentioned. D) 'take no time' is wrong: the passage does not say this.
rel: Inferior means worse or lower in quality; the opposite is superior. Both take 'to': inferior to, superior to.

question: "___ sun rises in the east."
facts: There is only one sun, so it takes the definite article 'The'. A) 'A' and B) 'An' are wrong: indefinite articles mean 'any one', but there is only one sun. D) is wrong: unique objects need 'the'.
rel: Other unique things with 'the': the moon, the earth, the sky, the world, the north pole.

question: Choose the synonym of LACK.
facts: Lack means not having enough; its synonym is Deficiency. A) Abundance, C) Excess and D) Plenty are wrong: they mean a lot, the opposite of lack.
rel: Other synonyms: shortage, want, dearth, scarcity. Antonym: abundance (see sa-3).

question: "He is ___ MBA graduate."
facts: We go by sound: the letter M is said 'em', which starts with a vowel sound, so 'an MBA graduate'. A) 'a' is wrong: 'a' is for consonant sounds. C) 'the' is wrong: no specific graduate is meant. D) is wrong: a singular countable noun needs an article.
rel: Other letters starting with vowel sounds: an MA, an MP, an LLB, an X-ray, an SP. But: a BA, a PhD (pee), a UN officer (yoo).

question: "Obsolete" means:
facts: B is right: obsolete means outdated and no longer in use. A) 'newly invented' is wrong: it is the opposite (novel, modern). C) 'expensive' is wrong: that is about price. D) 'dangerous' is wrong: that means risky.
rel: Synonyms of obsolete: outdated, out of date, antiquated, defunct. Antonyms: modern, current, up-to-date. Example: typewriters are now obsolete.

question: Synonym of "commence" is:
facts: 'Commence' is a formal word meaning to start, so 'begin' is the synonym. A) 'end' is the opposite. C) 'avoid' means to keep away from. D) 'reduce' means to make less.
rel: Other synonyms: start, initiate, launch. Antonyms: end, conclude, terminate. Noun: commencement.

question: Which contains an auxiliary verb?
facts: In "He has finished", "has" is a helping (auxiliary) verb used with the main verb "finished" to make the present perfect tense. A) "Birds fly" has only one main verb, "fly". C) "Tall trees grow" has only the main verb "grow". D) "Silence helps" has only the main verb "helps".
rel: The main auxiliary verbs are be (is, am, are, was, were), have (has, have, had) and do (do, does, did). Modals like can, will, must and should are also auxiliaries: "She can swim."

question: "Plausible" means:
facts: A is right: 'plausible' means something seems reasonable or believable. B) 'obviously impossible' is the opposite. C) 'very loud' is unrelated (that is 'loud' or 'deafening'). D) 'completely proven' is too strong; plausible only seems true, it is not proven.
rel: Synonyms: believable, credible, likely. Antonyms: implausible, unlikely, far-fetched.

question: Antonym of "rigid" is:
facts: 'Rigid' means stiff and not able to bend or change, so the antonym is 'flexible'. A) 'stiff' is a synonym. C) 'strict' is close to rigid (rigid rules). D) 'hard' is also close in meaning.
rel: Other antonyms: elastic, pliable, adaptable. Synonyms: inflexible, firm, unbending.

question: She was absent ___ class yesterday.
facts: The fixed phrase is "absent from" a place, class or duty. B) "of", C) "to" and D) "at" are not used with absent.
rel: Opposite: "present at" or "present in": "She was present at the meeting." Similar "from" phrases: different from, free from, safe from.

question: Which option contains a possessive pronoun?
facts: 'Mine' stands alone without a noun (The book is mine), so it is a possessive pronoun. A) 'my' is wrong: it must come before a noun (my book), so it is a possessive determiner/adjective. C) 'me' is wrong: it is an object pronoun. D) 'I' is wrong: it is a subject pronoun.
rel: Possessive pronouns: mine, yours, his, hers, ours, theirs. Their determiner pairs: my, your, his, her, our, their (used before nouns).

question: "Integrity" most nearly means:
facts: B is right: integrity means honesty and strong moral principles, moral uprightness. A) 'dishonesty' is wrong: it is the opposite. C) 'physical speed' is wrong: not related to morals. D) 'anger' is wrong: that is rage or fury.
rel: Synonyms of integrity: honesty, probity, rectitude, uprightness. Antonyms: dishonesty, corruption, deceit. Integrity can also mean wholeness, e.g. structural integrity.

question: Choose: "He studies at ___ university near his home."
facts: We choose "a" or "an" by sound, not by letter. "University" starts with a "yu" sound, which is a consonant sound, so we use "a". B) "an" is only for vowel sounds. C) "the" is for a particular university already known; here it is just any one university near his home. D) A singular countable noun needs an article, so "no article" is wrong.
rel: Similar words with "yu" or "w" sounds that take "a": a uniform, a European, a one-way street, a useful book.

question: Choose the antonym of DANGER.
facts: Danger means the chance of harm; its opposite is Safety. A) Hazard, C) Risk and D) Peril are wrong: they all mean danger.
rel: Other antonyms: security, protection, shelter. In sa-61, Risk is a synonym of danger.

question: "The cadets marched ___ the bridge."
facts: 'Across' means from one side to the other side, so they marched across the bridge. B) 'between' is wrong: it needs two things (between the two posts). C) 'during' is wrong: it is used with time, not place. D) 'since' is wrong: it is used for a point of time.
rel: Movement prepositions: across (side to side), through (inside, end to end), along (lengthwise), over (above), into (entering).

question: Choose the antonym of APPROVAL.
facts: Approval means agreeing that something is good or allowed; its opposite is Disapproval. A) Sanction, B) Assent and C) Consent are wrong: they all mean approval or permission.
rel: Other antonyms: rejection, refusal, disapprobation. In sa-64, Consent is a synonym of approval.

question: Read the passage: Efficient reading is not the same as reading every line at maximum speed. Skilled readers vary their pace according to purpose. They may scan a page to locate a date, skim an article to grasp its main argument, or read slowly when a paragraph contains dense reasoning. They also monitor comprehension. If a key sentence is unclear, they pause, reread, and connect it with surrounding ideas. This flexible approach is especially useful in timed tests, where spending too long on one difficult sentence can reduce the time available for easier questions.  QUESTION: In timed tests, spending too long on one sentence can:
facts: B is right: the passage says spending too long on one hard sentence 'can reduce the time available for easier questions'. A) is wrong: no automatic score increase is mentioned. C) is wrong: 'impossible forever' is extreme and not stated. D) is wrong: spending time does not guarantee understanding.
rel: Exam tip: options with extreme words like 'always', 'forever', 'guarantee', 'all' are usually wrong in reading questions.

question: Ali said, "I will come tomorrow."
options: Ali said that he would come the next day.
Ali said that I will come tomorrow.
Ali says that he would come yesterday.
Ali told he would came next day.
facts: 'Will' changes to 'would', 'I' to 'he', and 'tomorrow' to 'the next day': Ali said that he would come the next day. B) keeps 'I', 'will' and 'tomorrow'. C) uses 'says' and 'yesterday', which changes the meaning. D) 'told he' needs an object, and 'would came' is wrong; after 'would' use the base form 'come'.
rel: Other time changes: today becomes that day, yesterday becomes the previous day, next week becomes the following week.

question: "We ___ dinner when the phone rang."
facts: A longer action (having dinner) was going on when a short action (the phone rang) interrupted it, so past continuous 'were having' is right. A) 'had' is wrong: it suggests a complete action, not one in progress. C) 'have had' is wrong: present perfect does not fit a past story. D) 'will have' is wrong: it is future.
rel: Pattern: past continuous + when + simple past. Example: I was sleeping when the alarm rang. 'While' often goes with the longer action.

question: "Ambiguous" means:
options: having more than one possible meaning
facts: B is right: ambiguous means having more than one possible meaning, so it is not clear. A) 'clear' is wrong: it is the opposite. C) 'certain' is wrong: ambiguous suggests doubt, not certainty. D) 'short' is wrong: that is about length.
rel: Synonyms of ambiguous: unclear, vague, equivocal, open to interpretation. Antonyms: clear, explicit, unambiguous. Noun: ambiguity.

question: Synonym of "evaluate" is:
facts: "Evaluate" means to judge or measure the value or quality of something, so its synonym is "assess". B) "ignore" means to pay no attention, which is the opposite. C) "hide" means to keep out of sight. D) "destroy" means to ruin completely.
rel: Other synonyms of evaluate: appraise, judge, rate, examine. Noun form: evaluation ("a performance evaluation").

question: Choose the synonym of LUCK.
facts: Luck means what happens to a person by chance; Lot (fate, one's fortune in life) is the synonym. A) Effort, B) Plan and D) Labour are wrong: they mean things done on purpose by hard work, not chance.
rel: Other synonyms: fortune, fate, destiny, chance. Phrase: to be content with one's lot.

question: She said, "Hurrah! We have won."
options: She exclaimed with joy that they had won.
She exclaimed with sorrow that they won.
She said hurrah we have won.
She ordered that they had won.
facts: 'Hurrah' shows happiness, so we use 'exclaimed with joy', and 'we have won' becomes 'they had won': She exclaimed with joy that they had won. B) 'with sorrow' is the wrong feeling and 'won' should be 'had won'. C) keeps the exact words, which is direct, not indirect speech. D) 'ordered' is for commands, not exclamations.
rel: Similar: He said, 'Bravo! Well done' becomes He applauded me, saying that I had done well. 'Alas' takes 'with sorrow'.

question: Choose the antonym of AGREE.
facts: Agree means to have the same opinion; its opposite is Disagree. B) Consent, C) Approve and D) Accept are wrong: they all mean to agree.
rel: Prefix dis- makes the opposite: agree - disagree, approve - disapprove, like - dislike.

question: "He has lived here ___ 2022."
facts: Use 'since' with a point of time (2022) when the action continues to now. A) 'for' is wrong: 'for' is for a period (for three years). C) 'from only' is wrong: 'from' needs 'to/till' and does not suit present perfect. D) 'during' is wrong: it means within a period.
rel: Since + point of time: since Monday, since morning, since 2010. For + period: for two days, for a week, for ten years.

question: Choose the antonym of PRAISE.
facts: Praise means to say good things about someone; its opposite is Censure (strong criticism). B) Admire, C) Laud and D) Applaud are wrong: they all mean to praise or show approval.
rel: Other antonyms: blame, condemn, criticize. In sa-86, Laud is a synonym of praise.

question: "Now" commonly changes to:
facts: In reported speech, 'now' usually changes to 'then'. B) 'tomorrow' becomes 'the next day'; it is not a change for 'now'. C) 'there' is the change for 'here', a place word. D) 'before' is the change for 'ago', not for 'now'.
rel: Other changes: ago becomes before, tonight becomes that night, here becomes there.

question: She is taller ___ her sister.
facts: B is right: comparatives like 'taller' are followed by 'than'. A) 'then' is wrong: 'then' means 'after that' or 'at that time'. C) 'to' is wrong: 'to' is used only with Latin comparatives like senior to, superior to. D) 'from' is wrong: it is not used after comparatives in English.
rel: Remember: than = comparison, then = time. Example: 'He is older than me. We ate, then we left.' Latin words: senior to, junior to, prefer to.

question: Indirect: She said to him, "Please sit down."
options: She requested him to sit down.
She asked that he sat down.
facts: A polite request with "please" is reported with "requested" + object + to-infinitive, and "please" is dropped: "She requested him to sit down." B) "said him" is wrong ("said" takes "to": said to him) and it keeps "please". C) "asked that he sat down" is not the right pattern for a command. D) "ordered" is too strong for a polite request, and "sitting" should be "to sit".
rel: For orders use ordered or commanded: He said, "Close the door" becomes He ordered me to close the door. For negative requests: requested him not to go.

question: "She ___ already ___ the form."
facts: Present perfect is has/have + past participle, and 'already' comes between them: 'has already submitted'. B) 'had submit' is wrong: 'submit' is not a past participle. C) 'is submitted' is wrong: it is passive and does not fit 'She ... the form'. D) 'was submit' is wrong: 'was' with a base verb is not correct grammar.
rel: Words like already, just, never, ever, yet go with present perfect: He has just arrived. Have you ever seen snow? I haven't finished yet.

question: Passive of "They have postponed the match" is:
facts: The active is present perfect, so the passive is has/have been + past participle: "The match has been postponed." B) "had postpone" uses the wrong tense and the base form. C) "is postponing" is active present continuous. D) "was postponing" is active past continuous, not passive.
rel: Same rule: "She has written the report" becomes "The report has been written by her." The doer "by them" is often dropped when it is general.

question: Choose the antonym of WILD.
facts: Wild means not tamed, savage; its opposite is Civilized. A) Fierce, B) Untamed and C) Savage are wrong: they all mean the same as wild.
rel: Other antonyms of wild: tame, gentle, domesticated. In sa-58, Savage is a synonym of wild.

question: Passive of "Open the door" is best expressed as:
options: Let open the door by you.
facts: Imperative sentences (orders) become passive with 'Let + object + be + past participle': Let the door be opened. B) 'The door open' has no 'be' and no passive form. C) 'Door is opened you' is broken grammar with no 'by'. D) 'Let open the door by you' has wrong word order and no 'be'.
rel: Same rule: Close the window becomes Let the window be closed. For requests you can also say: You are requested to close the window.

question: I ___ him yesterday at the library.
facts: "Yesterday" is a finished past time, so we use the simple past "met". A) "meet" is present tense and does not fit a past time. B) "have met" is present perfect, which is not used with a definite past time like yesterday. D) "am meeting" is present continuous and shows now or the future, not yesterday.
rel: Other definite past time words that need simple past: last week, ago, in 2010, last night. Example: "I saw him two days ago" (not "have seen").

question: Choose the synonym of WILD.
facts: Wild means untamed and fierce; its synonym is Savage. B) Gentle, C) Civilized and D) Tame are wrong: they are opposite in meaning.
rel: Other synonyms: untamed, fierce, ferocious. Antonym: civilized (see sa-23).

question: Take an umbrella ___ it rains.
facts: A is right: 'in case' shows a precaution against something that may happen. B) 'although' is wrong: it shows contrast. C) 'because of' is wrong: it must be followed by a noun, not a clause. D) 'despite' is wrong: it shows contrast and also needs a noun.
rel: In case is followed by present tense for the future: 'Take a map in case you get lost.' Compare 'if': 'Take an umbrella if it rains' means only take it when it rains.

question: Choose the antonym of JUSTICE.
facts: Justice means fairness; its opposite is Inequity (unfairness). A) Honesty, C) Equity and D) Fairness are wrong: they are close in meaning to justice.
rel: Do not confuse inequity (unfairness) with iniquity (wickedness). Other antonyms of justice: injustice, unfairness.

question: The word "resilient" most nearly means:
facts: A is right: resilient means able to recover quickly from difficulty or shock. B) 'easily broken' is wrong: that is fragile, the opposite. C) 'unwilling to learn' is wrong: that is stubborn or obstinate. D) 'extremely noisy' is wrong: that is boisterous or deafening.
rel: Synonyms of resilient: tough, hardy, buoyant, adaptable. Antonyms: fragile, vulnerable. Noun: resilience.

question: Read the passage: Errors are unavoidable in serious learning. Their value, however, depends on what happens after they are noticed. Repeating an error without analysis produces little improvement. Effective learners identify the cause, correct the method, and test the correction under similar conditions. They also distinguish between a careless mistake and a conceptual misunderstanding. The first may require better attention; the second may require rebuilding knowledge from the foundation. This process can feel slower than simply doing more questions, but it usually produces more durable progress because it changes the mechanism that caused the failure.  QUESTION: The passage argues that errors become useful when learners:
facts: B is right: the passage says effective learners 'identify the cause, correct the method, and test the correction'. A) 'ignore them' is wrong: the passage says to analyse errors. C) 'repeat more questions immediately' is wrong: 'Repeating an error without analysis produces little improvement.' D) 'avoid difficult topics' is wrong: it is not suggested.
rel: Analyse means study carefully to find causes. Key idea: learning comes from understanding mistakes, not just practising more.

question: Synonym of "allocate" is:
facts: A is right: 'allocate' means to give or assign something for a purpose, e.g. allocate funds for schools. B) 'remove' is almost the opposite. C) 'hide' is unrelated. D) 'oppose' means to be against.
rel: Synonyms: assign, distribute, allot, earmark. Noun: allocation (budget allocation).

question: "She bought ___ umbrella and ___ raincoat."
facts: 'Umbrella' starts with a vowel sound, so 'an umbrella'; 'raincoat' starts with a consonant sound, so 'a raincoat'. A) 'a / a' is wrong: 'a umbrella' is incorrect. C) 'the / an' is wrong: 'an raincoat' is incorrect and no specific umbrella is meant. D) 'an / an' is wrong for the same reason.
rel: Quick check: an apple, an egg, an idea, an orange, an umbrella; a bag, a pen, a raincoat.

question: Choose the synonym of DISCLOSE.
facts: Disclose means to make known a secret; its synonym is Reveal. B) Hide, C) Cover and D) Conceal are wrong: they mean keep secret, the opposite.
rel: Other synonyms: expose, divulge, uncover. Antonyms: conceal, hide.

question: "Coherent" means:
facts: A is right: coherent means logical and well connected, easy to follow. B) 'broken physically' is wrong: coherent is about ideas, not physical damage. C) 'secret' is wrong: that is covert or confidential. D) 'angry' is wrong: that is irate.
rel: Synonyms of coherent: logical, consistent, lucid, clear. Antonyms: incoherent, confused, disjointed. Related: cohesion, cohesive (sticking together).

question: She said, "Where are you going?"
options: She asked where was I going.
She asked where I was going.
She said where I am going.
She asked that where I went.
facts: A wh-question keeps the wh-word but uses statement order (subject before verb): She asked where I was going. A) keeps question order 'was I'. C) uses 'said' and present 'am', with no tense change. D) 'asked that where' is wrong; do not add 'that', and 'went' changes the tense wrongly.
rel: Same rule: He said, 'What is your name?' becomes He asked what my name was. Subject comes before the verb in reported questions.

question: Choose the synonym of TROTH.
facts: Troth is an old word meaning faith, loyalty or a promise; so Faith is the synonym. A) Doubt, B) Betrayal and D) Treachery are wrong: they mean distrust or disloyalty, the opposite.
rel: Betroth (to promise in marriage) comes from troth. Other synonyms: fidelity, loyalty, pledge.

question: Choose the antonym of ACCUSATION.
facts: An accusation is a charge that someone did wrong; its opposite is Defence (speaking to protect oneself against the charge). B) Allegation, C) Charge and D) Blame are wrong: they all mean the same as accusation.
rel: Accuse (verb) - defend (verb). Other related words: vindication, exoneration (being cleared of blame).

question: Active of "English is spoken in many countries" is:
options: People speak English in many countries.
People spoke English in many countries only.
Many countries are speaking English people.
facts: 'Is spoken' is simple present passive with no agent, so the active uses a general subject in simple present: People speak English in many countries. B) 'spoke' is past tense and 'only' adds a new meaning. C) 'English speaks people' reverses the meaning. D) is wrong tense (continuous) and broken word order.
rel: When no agent is given, use people, someone or they as subject. Example: Rice is grown in Punjab becomes People grow rice in Punjab.

question: She ___ for the interview when I called.
facts: When one past action was in progress and another past action happened in the middle of it, the longer action takes the past continuous: "was preparing". A) "prepared" is simple past and shows a completed action, not one in progress. C) "has prepared" is present perfect and does not match the past clause "when I called". D) "will prepare" is future and does not fit a past event.
rel: Same pattern: "I was reading when the lights went out." The longer action uses was/were + verb-ing; the short action that interrupts uses simple past.

question: In "He is extremely careful," "extremely" modifies:
facts: 'Extremely' is an intensifier that tells how careful he is, so it modifies the adjective 'careful'. A) 'He' is wrong: adverbs do not modify pronouns. B) 'is' is wrong: it does not tell how he 'is'; it grades the quality. D) is wrong: it modifies one word, not the whole sentence.
rel: Adverbs can modify adjectives (very tall), other adverbs (very quickly) and verbs (ran quickly). Other intensifiers: very, too, quite, highly, fairly.

question: Choose the antonym of SIN.
facts: Sin means a wrong or evil act; its opposite is Virtue (goodness). A) Crime, C) Evil and D) Wrongdoing are wrong: they all mean the same as sin.
rel: Other antonyms: goodness, merit, righteousness. In sa-48, Crime is a synonym of sin.

question: Choose the antonym of FLEXIBLE.
facts: Flexible means easy to bend or change; its opposite is Rigid (stiff, cannot bend). A) Pliable, B) Supple and D) Elastic are wrong: they all mean bendable, so they are synonyms.
rel: Other antonyms of flexible: stiff, inflexible, unbending. Synonyms: pliant, bendable.

question: Choose the antonym of QUESTIONABLE.
facts: Questionable means doubtful, not certain; its opposite is Unquestionable (certain, beyond doubt). A) Doubtful, C) Dubious and D) Uncertain are wrong: they all mean the same as questionable.
rel: Other antonyms: certain, sure, undeniable, indisputable. Prefix un- makes the opposite: questionable - unquestionable.

question: "Meticulous" means:
facts: B is right: meticulous means very careful about every small detail. A) 'careless' is wrong: it is the opposite. C) 'lazy' is wrong: that is idle or indolent. D) 'fearful' is wrong: that means afraid.
rel: Synonyms of meticulous: painstaking, scrupulous, thorough, punctilious. Antonyms: careless, sloppy, negligent.

question: "Contingency" most nearly means:
options: a possible future event or emergency
facts: A is right: a contingency is a possible future event or emergency that you prepare for. B) 'a fixed certainty' is wrong: contingency means something that may or may not happen. C) 'a celebration' is wrong: that is a festivity. D) 'a routine fact only' is wrong: a contingency is unplanned, not routine.
rel: Related: contingency plan (a backup plan), contingent on (depending on): 'Promotion is contingent on results.' Synonyms: eventuality, possibility, emergency.

question: He studied hard; ___, he passed the test.
facts: B is right: passing the test is the result of studying hard, so 'therefore' fits. A) 'however' is wrong: it shows contrast. C) 'otherwise' is wrong: it means 'if not', giving a bad result. D) 'nevertheless' is wrong: it shows contrast, but here there is cause and effect.
rel: Other result linkers: thus, hence, consequently, as a result, so. Contrast linkers: however, nevertheless, nonetheless, yet.

question: Which is an adverb of manner?
facts: A is right: an adverb of manner tells HOW something is done, and 'carefully' tells how. B) 'yesterday' is an adverb of time (when). C) 'often' is an adverb of frequency (how often). D) 'outside' is an adverb of place (where).
rel: Many adverbs of manner end in -ly: quickly, slowly, loudly. Some do not: fast, hard, well (She sings well).

question: Antonym of "ancient" is:
facts: 'Ancient' means very old, from long ago, so the antonym is 'modern' (new, of present times). A) 'old' is a synonym. B) 'historic' is about the past, close in meaning. D) 'former' means earlier, also close in meaning, not opposite.
rel: Other antonyms: new, recent, contemporary. Synonyms of ancient: antique, archaic, primeval.

question: "She wants to become ___ engineer."
facts: 'Engineer' begins with a vowel sound, so it takes 'an'. A) 'a' is wrong: 'a' comes before consonant sounds. C) 'the' is wrong: she wants to be any one engineer, not a specific one. D) is wrong: a singular countable noun of profession needs an article.
rel: Professions take a/an: She is a doctor. He is an officer. He wants to be an architect.

question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: He is capable to do it.
He is capable of doing it.
He is capable for do it.
facts: The correct pattern is "capable of" + verb-ing: "He is capable of doing it." A) "capable to do" is a common mistake; capable does not take a to-infinitive. C) "capable for do" uses the wrong preposition and the base verb. D) "He capable of do it" has no verb "is" and uses "do" instead of "doing".
rel: Compare: "able to do" uses to-infinitive (He is able to do it), but "capable of doing" uses -ing. Similar: fond of reading, good at swimming.

question: Choose the correct sentence.
facts: "Police" is a plural noun even without "s", so it takes the plural verb: "The police are investigating." A) "is" is singular, so it is wrong. C) "are investigates" is wrong grammar: after "are" we use the -ing form. D) "A police" is wrong: we cannot use "a" with police; we say "a police officer".
rel: Other nouns that are always plural: cattle, people, clothes, scissors, trousers. Example: "The cattle are grazing."

question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: I look forward to meet you.
I look forward to meeting you.
I look forward for meet you.
I am look forward to meeting you.
facts: In "look forward to", the word "to" is a preposition, not part of an infinitive, so it is followed by verb-ing: "I look forward to meeting you." A) "to meet" wrongly treats "to" as an infinitive. C) "for meet" uses the wrong preposition and the base verb. D) "am look" is wrong grammar; it should be "I am looking forward".
rel: Other phrases where "to" is a preposition and takes -ing: be used to, object to, be committed to, get used to. Example: "I am used to waking up early."

question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: She has less books than me.
She has fewer books than I do.
She has lesser books than I.
facts: B is right: 'books' can be counted, so we use 'fewer', and 'than I do' is correct (I have books). A) 'less' is for uncountable nouns like water or sugar, not books. C) 'lesser' means lower in importance, not smaller in number. D) 'She have' is wrong: with 'she' we use 'has'.
rel: Fewer time, less water: fewer is for things you count (fewer chairs), less is for things you cannot count (less money). Compare: 'He is taller than I am' or 'taller than me' in informal English.

question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: He denied to take the money.
facts: B is right: the verb 'deny' is followed by a gerund (verb + ing), so 'denied taking'. A) 'deny to take' is wrong: 'deny' does not take 'to' + verb. C) 'denied take' is wrong: a bare verb cannot follow 'deny'. D) 'denied that taking' is wrong: 'that' needs a full clause like 'that he took'.
rel: Other verbs followed by -ing: admit, avoid, enjoy, finish, mind, suggest (He admitted stealing). You can also say 'He denied that he had taken the money.'

question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: She is one of the best player.
She is one of the best players.
She is one of best players is.
She one of the best player.
facts: B is right: 'one of the' + superlative is followed by a plural noun: 'one of the best players'. A) 'player' is singular, which is wrong after 'one of the'. C) extra 'is' at the end and missing 'the' make it wrong. D) it has no verb ('is') and uses a singular noun.
rel: Same rule: one of my friends, one of the tallest buildings. The verb stays singular: One of the boys is absent.

question: Choose the correct sentence.
facts: B is right: 'candidates' is a plural countable noun, so we use 'are fewer'. A) 'less' is for uncountable nouns, not candidates. C) 'is' does not agree with plural 'candidates'. D) 'lesser' is wrong here and 'candidate' should be plural.
rel: Fewer students, less homework. Also: 'a number of' (countable) versus 'an amount of' (uncountable).

question: Choose the correct sentence.
facts: With 'does not', the main verb stays in the base form: He does not know me. A) 'He do not' is wrong; 'he' takes 'does', not 'do'. B) 'does not knows' is wrong; after 'does' do not add -s. D) 'not does know' has wrong word order.
rel: Same rule: She does not like tea. Did not also takes base form: He did not go (not 'did not went').

question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: She is more senior than me always.
facts: Latin comparatives like senior, junior, superior, inferior, prior take 'to', not 'than': She is senior to me. A) 'senior than' is a common mistake. C) 'senior from' is wrong. D) 'more senior than' is wrong here, and 'always' adds extra meaning.
rel: Similar: He is junior to me. This is superior to that. Also: prefer to, prior to.

question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: Neither of the boys are absent.
Neither of the boys is absent.
facts: 'Neither of' + plural noun takes a singular verb: Neither of the boys is absent. A) 'are' is the plural verb, wrong here. C) 'Neither boys' is wrong; without 'of', neither takes a singular noun (neither boy). D) misses 'the' and uses plural 'are'.
rel: Same rule with either, each, every one: Either of the answers is correct. Each of them is ready.

question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: Each of the players have a kit.
Each of the players has a kit.
Each of players have a kit.
facts: 'Each of' + plural noun takes a singular verb: Each of the players has a kit. A) 'have' is plural, wrong here. C) 'Each players' is wrong; without 'of', 'each' takes a singular noun, and 'a' is missing. D) misses 'the' and uses plural 'have'.
rel: Same rule: Every student has a book. Each of the girls is talented.

question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: He has been living here since five years.
He has been living here for five years.
He is living here for five years ago.
He lived here since five years.
facts: Use 'for' with a period of time (five years) and 'since' with a point of time (2020): He has been living here for five years. A) 'since five years' is a common mistake. C) mixes present 'is living' with 'ago'. D) simple past 'lived' does not go with 'since'.
rel: Examples: since Monday, since 2019, since morning; for two hours, for a week, for ten years.

question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: I prefer tea over than coffee.
facts: 'Prefer' takes 'to', not 'than': I prefer tea to coffee. A) 'prefer than' is a common mistake. C) 'over than' mixes two forms and is wrong. D) 'prefer from' is wrong.
rel: With verbs: I prefer walking to driving. With 'would rather' we use 'than': I would rather walk than drive.

question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: One of my friend is here.
One of my friends is here.
One of my friends are here.
facts: 'One of' is followed by a plural noun, and the verb is singular because the subject is 'one': One of my friends is here. A) 'friend' must be plural after 'one of'. C) 'are' is wrong; the subject 'one' is singular. D) misses 'of'.
rel: Same rule: One of the students is absent. One of the best players has left.
